question: A patient with confirmed primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) and no contraindications requires pharmacological IOP lowering. Which drug class is the preferred first-line topical agent, and why is it NOT used as first-line in acute angle-closure crisis?

answers.text: Topical beta-blockers (e.g. timolol), because they reduce aqueous production; avoided in angle-closure because they cause miosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Beta-blockers do reduce aqueous production and are commonly used in POAG, but they are NOT avoided in PACG because of miosis. Also, beta-blockers are NOT the recommended first-line class in POAG — prostaglandin analogues are preferred for their 24-hour IOP profile and once-daily dosing.

answers.text: Prostaglandin analogues (e.g. latanoprost), because they enhance uveoscleral outflow; not used acutely in angle-closure because they require weeks to act and do not immediately break pupil block

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost, bimatoprost, travoprost) are the preferred first-line agents in POAG — they increase uveoscleral outflow by 35-50%, are dosed once nightly, and have excellent 24-hour IOP control. In acute PACG, the priority is immediate IOP crisis control (acetazolamide IV, mannitol IV, pilocarpine to break pupil block) then definitive laser PI — PGAs are too slow and do not address the mechanical angle closure.

answers.text: Pilocarpine (miotic), because it opens the trabecular meshwork; first-line in both POAG and PACG

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pilocarpine constricts the pupil and pulls the peripheral iris away from the trabecular meshwork — it IS used in acute PACG to break pupil block. However, it is NOT first-line in POAG (side effects: miosis, dim vision, headache) and is not used in POAG as a preferred agent. It is emphatically NOT first-line in POAG by current guidelines.

answers.text: Systemic acetazolamide, because it rapidly reduces aqueous production; contraindicated in PACG due to renal toxicity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Acetazolamide is actually used in BOTH POAG and PACG. In acute PACG crisis, IV/oral acetazolamide is part of the emergency protocol. It is not first-line in chronic POAG management. And its contraindication in PACG is not renal toxicity — it is used in the acute attack.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: POAG is treated long-term with prostaglandin analogues first-line. Acute PACG is an emergency requiring pilocarpine (pupil constriction to break pupil block) + IV acetazolamide + IV mannitol, then definitive laser peripheral iridotomy — not prostaglandins.

Key distinction secured: POAG → prostaglandin analogues first-line (uveoscleral outflow enhancement). Acute PACG → pilocarpine + acetazolamide + mannitol (emergency break of pupil block) then laser PI.
